claim: Neuromodulatory nuclei that are part of the ascending arousal system (AAS) play a crucial role in regulating cortical state and optimizing task performance.
source: Neuromodulatory nuclei that are part of the ascending arousal system (AAS) play a crucial role in regulating cortical state and optimizing task performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Bunzeck and Düzel, 2006; de Gee et al., 2017; Shine et al., 2021; Thiele and Bellgrove, 2018) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Pupil diameter, under constant luminance conditions, is increasingly used as an index of activity of AAS nuclei.
source: Pupil diameter, under constant luminance conditions, is increasingly used as an index of activity of these AAS nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Joshi and Gold, 2020.

claim: Task-based functional imaging studies in humans have begun to provide evidence of stimulus-driven pupil-AAS coupling.
source: Indeed, task-based functional imaging studies in humans have begun to provide evidence of stimulus-driven pupil-AAS coupling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research as indicated in the Abstract.

claim: Activation in all six AAS nuclei was optimally correlated with pupil size at 0–2 s lags.
source: Activation in all six AAS nuclei was optimally correlated with pupil size at 0–2 s lags, suggesting that spontaneous pupil changes were almost immediately followed by corresponding BOLD-signal changes in the AAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the study, specifically the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Spontaneous pupil changes were almost immediately followed by corresponding BOLD-signal changes in the AAS.
source: Activation in all six AAS nuclei was optimally correlated with pupil size at 0–2 s lags, suggesting that spontaneous pupil changes were almost immediately followed by corresponding BOLD-signal changes in the AAS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the 0-2s lag correlation data presented in the study.

claim: Spontaneous changes in pupil size that occur during states of rest can be used as a noninvasive general index of activity in AAS nuclei.
source: These results suggest that spontaneous changes in pupil size that occur during states of rest can be used as a noninvasive general index of activity in AAS nuclei.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing correlations between pupil size and AAS BOLD activity.

claim: The nature of pupil-AAS coupling during rest appears to be vastly different from the relatively slow canonical hemodynamic response function that has been used to characterize task-related pupil-AAS coupling.
source: Importantly, the nature of pupil-AAS coupling during rest appears to be vastly different from the relatively slow canonical hemodynamic response function that has been used to characterize task-related pupil-AAS coupling.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings showing optimal correlations at 0-2s lags rather than the typical 5-6s HRF.

claim: Task-related activity of AAS nuclei is accompanied by changes in pupil size and its first-order derivative.
source: Indeed, task-related activity of these nuclei is accompanied by changes in pupil size and its first-order derivative (i.e., rate of change), as evidenced by animal studies and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies in humans (Cazettes et al., 2021; de Gee et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2014; Varazzani et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Animal studies have found pupil-AAS coupling of spontaneous fluctuations during rest.
source: Animal studies have also found pupil-AAS coupling of spontaneous fluctuations during rest (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: It is still largely unclear whether similar coupling can be found between resting-state fluctuations of pupil size and blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals in the human AAS.
source: However, it is still largely unclear whether similar coupling can be found between resting-state fluctuations of pupil size and blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals in the human AAS.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on review of existing literature.

claim: The majority of previous human resting-state fMRI studies did not focus on the AAS.
source: However, the majority of these studies did not focus on the AAS.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' review of previous literature.

claim: Previous studies did not include specific localization methods to delineate AAS regions of interest (ROIs) or correct for physiological sources of noise.
source: Moreover, they did not include specific localization methods to delineate AAS regions of interest (ROIs) or correct for physiological sources of noise, such as cardiac and respiratory fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' review of previous literature.

claim: Specific localization methods and physiological noise correction are important for reliable measurements in subcortical nuclei.
source: These approaches are important for reliable measurements in these subcortical nuclei (Brooks et al., 2013; Matt et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: Murphy et al., 2014 found a positive coupling between fluctuations in pupil size and activation in the LC during rest.
source: The authors found a positive coupling between fluctuations in pupil size and activation in the LC during rest.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to Murphy et al., 2014.

claim: There have been no human fMRI studies so far that have reported a relationship between pupil size and other AAS nuclei during rest.
source: To our knowledge, there have been no human fMRI studies so far that have reported a relationship between pupil size and other AAS nuclei during rest, despite the growing evidence from animal studies (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016) speaking for such a relationship.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' review of existing literature.

claim: The study examined simultaneous measurements of resting-state fMRI and pupil size from 74 healthy adults.
source: To address this aim, we systematically examined simultaneous measurements of resting-state fMRI and pupil size from a large sample of healthy adults (N = 74).
evidence: This claim describes the study design and sample size.

claim: The study monitored BOLD signal from the LC, VTA, SN, DR, MR, and BF.
source: We monitored BOLD signal from a number of subcortical nuclei part of the AAS and implicated in the control of cortical arousal levels: the LC, the ventral tegmental area (VTA), dopaminergic substantia nigra (SN), the dorsal (DR) and median (MR) raphe nuclei, and the nucleus basalis of Meynert in the cholinergic basal forebrain (BF).
evidence: This claim describes the ROIs examined in the study.

claim: Studying small subcortical nuclei using fMRI comes with a unique set of challenges due to their size and location in the brain.
source: Due to their size and location in the brain, studying these small nuclei using fMRI comes with a unique set of challenges (Forstmann et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Matt et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: Multi-echo imaging can increase signal-to-noise ratio in subcortical structures.
source: Here, we mitigated these challenges by implementing a number of methods, including multi-echo imaging to increase signal-to-noise ratio in subcortical structures (Miletić et al., 2020; Puckett et al., 2018; Turker et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: Neuromelanin-weighted T1 imaging can be used for delineation of the LC.
source: neuromelanin-weighted T1 imaging for delineation of the LC (Clewett et al., 2016; Keren et al., 2015; Mäki-Marttunen and Espeseth, 2021; Priovoulos et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: The study replicated whole-brain pupil-BOLD patterns consistent with Schneider et al., 2016.
source: First, following the approach by Schneider et al., 2016, we used pupil size (1 s shift) as a regressor in a GLM and convolved it with the canonical HRF (i.e., 6 s TTP). The assumption here is that the neural activity associated with spontaneous changes in pupil size is transformed into resting-state BOLD signal according to the same impulse response function as that driving neurovascular coupling during task performance. Indeed, we found positive correlations in the thalamus and negative correlations in the visual cortex and sensorimotor areas, as well as in the precuneus, cuneus, insula, superior temporal gyrus, and parahippocampal gyrus. These patterns of activation are consistent with those reported by Schneider et al., 2016 (Figure 1A and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: The study found significant clusters in the visual cortex, the insula, the anterior cingulate gyrus, and the inferior frontal gyrus, consistent with Murphy et al., 2014.
source: Here, we found significant clusters in the visual cortex, the insula, the anterior cingulate gyrus, and the inferior frontal gyrus, consistent with what was reported by Murphy et al., 2014.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and comparison to previous work.

claim: The study was unable to replicate pupil-LC BOLD coupling using the same convolution methods as Murphy et al., 2014.
source: Thus, contrary to Murphy et al., 2014, we were unable to replicate pupil-LC BOLD coupling using the same convolution methods.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results showing no significant pupil-LC coupling.

claim: The average tSNR across the AAS ROIs ranged from 23.3 to 72.9.
source: The average tSNR across the AAS ROIs (Figure 2B; range: 23.3–72.9) and cortical regions (range: 49.6–106.3) were in line with previous reports (Brooks et al., 2013, Figure 1: brainstem range: ~1–50 and cortex range ~50–112; Singh et al., 2022, Figure 2B: brainstem range: 0–50, cortex range: 0–50).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2B and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The study replicated a pattern of positive (partial) correlations among the signal fluctuations in each pair of subcortical ROIs, controlled for activity in the pons.
source: We also replicated a recently reported pattern of positive (partial) correlations among the signal fluctuations in each pair of subcortical ROIs, controlled for activity in the pons (Figure 2C; van den Brink et al., 2019; see also Singh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous studies.

claim: The correlation between the DR and VTA was negative.
source: Only the correlation between the DR and VTA was negative.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The use of region- and participant-specific HRFs did not result in significant pupil-AAS coupling.
source: The pupil-BOLD analysis using these specific HRFs, however, revealed no significant pupil-AAS correlations (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Pupil size correlated negatively with activation in the OCC.
source: We only found that pupil size correlated negatively with activation in the OCC (pcorr<0.001 [pupil size], pcorr=0.018 [pupil derivative], false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data with statistical significance values.

claim: The TTP of the estimated HRFs was significantly faster for all subcortical AAS ROIs than for each of the two cortical ROIs.
source: After carrying out pairwise comparisons, we found that, as expected, the TTP of the estimated HRFs was significantly faster for all subcortical AAS ROIs than for each of the two cortical ROIs (Msubcortical ROIs = 4.7 s, SDsubcortical ROIs = 0.6 s, Mcortical ROIs = 5.4 s, SDcortical ROIs = 0.8 s; Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3D with statistical comparisons.

claim: Subcortical structures have been characterized by faster BOLD responses (TTP 4–5 s) compared to the cortex (TTP 5–6 s).
source: Indeed, subcortical structures have been characterized by faster BOLD responses (TTP 4–5 s; Lau et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2018; Yen et al., 2011) compared to the cortex (TTP 5–6 s; Lewis et al., 2018; Friston et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: For almost all AAS ROIs the strength of pupil-BOLD coupling differed across TTPs.
source: We found that for almost all AAS ROIs the strength of pupil-BOLD coupling differed across TTPs (main effect of TTP; LC: p<0.001; VTA: p<0.001; SN: p<0.001; MR: p=0.043; BF: p=0.009, FDR-corrected for nine ROIs).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data with statistical significance values.

claim: Coupling between pupil size and AAS BOLD patterns increases with earlier TTPs.
source: The overall pattern shows that coupling between pupil size and AAS BOLD patterns increases with earlier TTPs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Positive correlations were found for all AAS regions at earlier TTPs (especially the 1 s and 2 s TTPs).
source: Specifically, we found positive correlations for all AAS regions at earlier TTPs (especially the 1 s [Figure 4B] and 2 s TTPs) but no significant correlations (LC, VTA, SN, DR, MR) at later TTPs (5–6 s; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For the OCC ROI, there was a positive correlation at the 1 s TTP, followed by a shift to negative correlations at later TTPs (4–6 s).
source: For the OCC ROI, we found a positive correlation at the 1 s TTP, followed by a shift to negative correlations at later TTPs (4–6 s), which is in line with previous work (Breeden et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2016; Yellin et al., 2015) and the results we reported above ('Whole-brain pupil-BOLD patterns consistent with previous studies').
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The ACC correlated positively with pupil size at predominantly early TTPs (1–4 s).
source: The ACC correlated positively with pupil size at predominantly early TTPs (1–4 s; Figure 4CD), similar to the AAS ROIs, and in line with pupil-BOLD coupling in default-mode network areas (Yellin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 4 and citation to previous work.

claim: Significant positive pupil-BOLD correlations were found for all AAS ROIs (except the DR), with the strongest correlations occurring at lag 0.
source: Critically, and in line with the TTP analysis, we found significant positive pupil-BOLD correlations for all AAS ROIs (except the DR), with the strongest correlations occurring at lag 0 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The relationship between pupil size and AAS activity is temporally close, rather than following the shape of an HRF with a 5 or 6 s TTP.
source: These results again suggest that the relationship between pupil size and AAS activity is temporally close, rather than following the shape of an HRF with a 5 or 6 s TTP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cross-correlation results showing strongest correlations at lag 0.

claim: Partialing out the contribution of the LC resulted in a slight but significant drop for the BF.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, partialing out the contribution of the LC resulted in a slight but significant drop for the BF (p=0.028).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 5C with statistical significance values.

claim: The signal from the VTA, SN, MR, and BF remained significantly correlated with pupil size after partialing out the LC contribution.
source: The signal from the VTA, SN, MR, and BF remained significantly correlated with pupil size (ps<0.030).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data with statistical significance values.

claim: Pupil size is not selectively driven by the LC, but a broader network of AAS nuclei is involved.
source: These results contribute further evidence to the notion that pupil size is not selectively driven by the LC, but that a broader network of AAS nuclei is involved.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the partial correlation analysis showing independent contributions of multiple AAS nuclei.

claim: The correlations for most AAS nuclei and both cortical ROIs were largely driven by frequencies between 0.04 and 0.09 Hz.
source: A simple peak detection indicated that the correlations for most AAS nuclei and both cortical ROIs (ACC and OCC) were largely driven by frequencies between 0.04 and 0.09 Hz (LC: 0.09; VTA: 0.04; SN: 0.03; DR: 0.008; MR: 0.04; BF: 0.04; ACC: 0.04; OCC: 0.07; Figure 6AB).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cross-spectral power density analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: A positive correlation was found between pupil size and BOLD signal in all of the AAS ROIs: LC, VTA, SN, DR, MR, and (sublenticular) BF.
source: In this study, we examined whether, during rest, non-luminance-related spontaneous fluctuations in pupil size were associated with fluctuations in BOLD signal in nuclei part of the AAS. We found a positive correlation between pupil size and BOLD signal in all of the AAS ROIs: LC, VTA, SN, DR, MR, and (sublenticular) BF.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the study.

claim: Pupil changes reflect activity in multiple neuromodulatory systems, not only the noradrenergic system.
source: This finding is in line with recent animal studies (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016) indicating that pupil changes reflect activity in multiple neuromodulatory systems, not only the noradrenergic system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to animal studies.

claim: During rest, unlike in response to task events, BOLD signal fluctuations in AAS nuclei immediately follow fluctuations in pupil size.
source: Critically, using two different methodological approaches, we found that pupil-AAS coupling was strongest when the two signals were assumed to occur close in time. This means that during rest, unlike in response to task events (de Gee et al., 2017), BOLD signal fluctuations in AAS nuclei immediately follow fluctuations in pupil size.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and comparison to previous task-based studies.

claim: The correlation between pupil size and AAS BOLD signal was largely driven by slow oscillations (~0.05–0.1 Hz) in both measures.
source: This correlation was largely driven by slow oscillations (i.e., ~0.05–0.1 Hz) in both measures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cross-spectral power density analysis.

claim: Pupil size can be used as a noninvasive readout of AAS activity.
source: Together, our results suggest that pupil size can be used as a noninvasive readout of AAS activity and reveal new insights into the temporal dynamics of pupil-AAS coupling during rest.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the overall experimental findings of the study.

claim: Robust positive correlations were found between pupil size and BOLD signal in five AAS ROIs: LC, VTA, SN, MR, and (sublenticular) BF.
source: We found robust positive correlations between pupil size and BOLD signal in five of our AAS ROIs: LC, VTA, SN, MR, and (sublenticular) BF.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the study.

claim: The correlations with the VTA, SN, MR, and BF BOLD signals remained significant after controlling for the effect of the LC BOLD signal.
source: The correlations with the VTA, SN, MR, and BF BOLD signals remained significant after controlling for the effect of the LC BOLD signal, suggesting that these AAS nuclei have independent influences on pupil size.
evidence: This claim is supported by the partial correlation analysis.

claim: The positive relationship with pupil size was less robust for the DR, and only significant in the TTP analyses.
source: The positive relationship with pupil size was less robust for the DR, and only significant in the TTP analyses, perhaps because this area had lower tSNR than the other subcortical ROIs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and speculation about the reason.

claim: The coupling between pupil size and activation of the AAS is not specific for the LC.
source: Thus, unlike what findings from previous studies (e.g., Murphy et al., 2014) may have implicitly suggested, the coupling between pupil size and activation of the AAS is not specific for the LC.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing correlations with multiple AAS nuclei.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the LC or DR increases pupil size.
source: Specifically, our findings are consistent with recent animal studies that found co-fluctuations in pupil size and LC and BF activity during rest (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016); with studies showing that optogenetic activation of the LC or DR increases pupil size (Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; Cazettes et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Human task-related fMRI work has shown positive correlations between event-related pupil responses and BOLD responses in the LC, VTA, and BF.
source: and with human task-related fMRI work showing positive correlations between event-related pupil responses and BOLD responses in the LC, VTA, and BF (de Gee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous human fMRI study.

claim: Changes in pupil size should not be used to infer a selective role for the LC.
source: However, our findings reinforce previous arguments (Joshi and Gold, 2020) that changes in pupil size should not be used to infer a selective role for the LC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citation to previous arguments.

claim: BOLD signal in the AAS closely followed the corresponding pupil fluctuations.
source: The temporal relationship between pupil size and AAS BOLD response patterns was different than we had expected based on reports from previous resting-state and event-related fMRI studies (de Gee et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2014). Namely, we found that BOLD signal in the AAS closely followed the corresponding pupil fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: Maximal and significant pupil-AAS coupling was found using HRFs with TTPs of 1–3 s.
source: Pupil time series that were convolved with the canonical HRF (TTP = 6 s) or region-specific HRFs based on a point process approach were not significantly related to AAS activation. Instead, maximal and significant pupil-AAS coupling was found using HRFs with TTPs of 1–3 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the TTP analysis.

claim: Cross-correlations between the unconvolved pupil time series and AAS BOLD time series revealed maximum correlations when the signals occurred close in time (at lags of 0–2 s).
source: In addition, cross-correlations between the unconvolved pupil time series and AAS BOLD time series similarly revealed maximum correlations when the signals occurred close in time (at lags of 0–2 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: Subcortical regions and AAS nuclei are characterized by faster event-related hemodynamic responses than cortical regions.
source: Our findings are in line with previous research that has suggested that subcortical regions (Lewis et al., 2018) and AAS nuclei (de Gee et al., 2017) are characterized by faster event-related hemodynamic responses than cortical regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the current experimental findings.

claim: Most previous human resting-state pupil-fMRI studies did not find or report pupil-AAS coupling because they only investigated pupil-BOLD coupling with longer time lags.
source: Furthermore, our findings may provide a reason why most previous human resting-state pupil-fMRI studies (e.g., Breeden et al., 2017; Schneider et al., 2016; Yellin et al., 2015) did not find or report pupil-AAS coupling. Namely, these studies only investigated pupil-BOLD coupling with longer time lags between pupil changes and corresponding BOLD response patterns.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the current findings and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The study broadly replicated previously reported associations between pupil size and cortical BOLD response patterns using standard TTPs.
source: Using standard TTPs, we (broadly) replicated previously reported associations between pupil size and cortical BOLD response patterns (e.g., negative coupling with the visual cortex, positive coupling with the thalamus and posterior cingulate cortex; e.g., Murphy et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2016; Yellin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The study did not find evidence that standard TTPs characterized the coupling between resting-state pupil size and AAS activation.
source: However, we did not find evidence that standard TTPs characterized the coupling between resting-state pupil size and AAS activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing no significant correlations at standard TTPs.

claim: A recent study in rats found temporally close positive coupling (i.e., 1 s TTP) between resting-state pupil dynamics and BOLD signal in specific areas in the brainstem including the A5 noradrenergic cell group.
source: Although we cannot make a direct comparison between the shape of human and mouse HRFs, a recent study in rats (Pais-Roldán et al., 2020) also found temporally close positive coupling (i.e., 1 s TTP) between resting-state pupil dynamics and BOLD signal in specific areas in the brainstem including the A5 noradrenergic cell group (which projects to the spinal cord).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an animal study.

claim: The rat study by Pais-Roldán et al., 2020 did not find evidence for a coupling between pupil dynamics and any of the AAS nuclei.
source: This study, however, did not find evidence for a coupling between pupil dynamics and any of the AAS nuclei.
evidence: This claim is based on citation to the animal study.

claim: Behavioral states can strongly modulate pupil-AAS coupling.
source: Preliminary evidence suggests that behavioral states can strongly modulate pupil-AAS coupling (Megemont et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to preliminary evidence.

claim: In an anesthetized state pupil-AAS coupling may be reduced or absent.
source: and therefore it is possible that in an anesthetized state pupil-AAS coupling is reduced or absent.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the preliminary evidence about behavioral state modulation.

claim: Ultra-slow (~0.1 Hz) BOLD fluctuations that are characteristic of resting-state fMRI data are entrained by ultra-slow vasomotor oscillations that lead to rhythmic changes in the diameter of brain arterioles.
source: Interestingly, recent work in the mouse cortex has shown that the ultra-slow (~0.1 Hz) BOLD fluctuations that are characteristic of resting-state fMRI data are entrained by ultra-slow vasomotor oscillations that lead to rhythmic changes in the diameter of brain arterioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work in mouse cortex.

claim: Vasomotor oscillations are entrained by rhythmic local neuronal activity in the same ultra-low-frequency band.
source: These vasomotor oscillations, in turn, are entrained by rhythmic local neuronal activity in the same ultra-low-frequency band (Drew et al., 2020; Mateo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the mouse brain the sequence from neuronal activity and vasomotion to blood oxygenation levels was estimated to last approximately 2.6 s.
source: However, in the mouse brain this sequence, from neuronal activity and vasomotion to blood oxygenation levels, was estimated to last approximately 2.6 s (Mateo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The EPI sequence had a higher spatial resolution (2 mm isotropic) than previous studies linking pupil size to BOLD.
source: First, although our EPI sequence had a higher spatial resolution (2 mm isotropic) than previous studies linking pupil size to BOLD (e.g., 3.5 mm isotropic in Murphy et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim describes the spatial resolution used in the study and compares it to previous work.

claim: Imaging small subcortical structures at conventional spatial resolution may have led to partial-volume averaging.
source: imaging small subcortical structures at this conventional spatial resolution may have led to partial-volume averaging (Forstmann et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017), especially in the LC, the smallest of our ROIs.
evidence: This is a potential limitation acknowledged by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: The study did not apply spatial smoothing to the EPI data.
source: To mitigate this concern, we did not apply spatial smoothing to the EPI data.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological choice made in the study.

claim: The LC showed the same pattern of results as other, much larger nuclei, including the VTA, SN, and BF.
source: Our confidence in the LC imaging data reported here is also bolstered by the fact that the LC showed the same pattern of results as other, much larger nuclei, including the VTA, SN, and BF, that are less susceptible to partial-volume averaging effects.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data showing consistent patterns across ROIs.

claim: A further increase in spatial resolution at 3T would be accompanied by a dramatic drop in signal-to-noise ratio.
source: We also note that a further increase in spatial resolution at 3T would be accompanied by a dramatic drop in signal-to-noise ratio (Murphy et al., 2007), and therefore would not per se lead to a better signal from the AAS regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The study included an extensive physiological noise correction model, accounting for measured cardiac and respiratory signal components as well as residual signal from the fourth ventricle.
source: To mitigate this concern, we included an extensive physiological noise correction model, accounting for measured cardiac and respiratory signal components as well as residual signal from the fourth ventricle.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: If the BOLD signal in AAS nuclei was largely driven by noise, this could not explain the robust temporal relationship between AAS BOLD and pupil size.
source: Furthermore, if the BOLD signal in AAS nuclei was largely driven by noise, this could not explain the robust temporal relationship between AAS BOLD and pupil size, and the selective absence of pupil-BOLD coupling in the pons, our control region that is also susceptible to physiological noise artifacts.
evidence: This is a logical argument based on the experimental findings.

claim: The analyses were limited by the temporal resolution of the fMRI data due to the 2 s TR.
source: A third drawback is that our analyses were limited by the temporal resolution of our fMRI data. Due to our 2 s TR, we were unable to interrogate potentially meaningful, faster pupil-BOLD correlations.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Spontaneous changes in pupil size that occur during rest reflect activity in a variety of nuclei that are part of the AAS.
source: In conclusion, we show that spontaneous changes in pupil size that occur during rest reflect activity in a variety of nuclei that are part of the AAS.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall experimental findings.

claim: Pupil size can be used as a noninvasive and general index of AAS activity, in contrast to previous work suggesting a selective role for the LC in arousal-related pupil size changes.
source: This suggests that pupil size can be used as a noninvasive and general index of AAS activity, in contrast to previous work suggesting a selective role for the LC in arousal-related pupil size changes.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall experimental findings and comparison to previous work.

claim: The findings provide new insights into the nature and temporal dynamics of AAS-linked pupil size fluctuations.
source: Together, our findings provide new insights into the nature and temporal dynamics of AAS-linked pupil size fluctuations.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall experimental findings.

claim: Seventy-four right-handed participants were recruited from New York University and completed two resting-state sessions on two consecutive days.
source: Seventy-four right-handed participants were recruited from New York University and completed two resting-state sessions on two consecutive days.
evidence: This claim describes the study sample and design.

claim: Two participants were excluded entirely and one session for one participant was excluded due to technical issues with the scanner, leaving a sample size of 72 participants.
source: Two participants were excluded entirely and one session for one participant was excluded due to technical issues with the scanner, leaving a sample size of 72 participants for the current study
evidence: This claim describes the final sample size after exclusions.

claim: Multi-echo EPI protocols can be used to avoid the tradeoff between BOLD sensitivity in the cortex and subcortex.
source: Multi-echo EPI protocols can be used to avoid the tradeoff between BOLD sensitivity in the cortex and subcortex (Turker et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous methodological study.

claim: Voxel-wise weighted sums of both echoes were calculated based on local contrast-to-noise ratio to account for regional variation in susceptibility-induced signal dropout.
source: To account for regional variation in susceptibility-induced signal dropout, voxel-wise weighted sums of both echoes were calculated based on local contrast-to-noise ratio (Poser et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim describes a methodological approach used in the study, supported by citation.

claim: ANTs SyN was found to be the best performing method for normalization.
source: Since ANTs SyN was found to be the best performing method for normalization (Ewert et al., 2019), some steps, including standardization and registration, were carried out using ANTs instead.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous methodological study.
